title: Chronic Headache in a Teenager on Acne Medication (Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension)
patient_instructions: You are the parent of Samantha, a 15-year-old girl, and you attend because her headaches have gone on for several weeks and are not improving. Samantha is mildly overweight. If asked about the headache on her behalf: it is on both sides, dull, present most days and slowly worsening, with some nausea. The KEY details, given only if asked specifically: she has noticed blurred vision and occasional DOUBLE VISION, and sometimes hears a 'whooshing/buzzing' noise in her ears. No early-morning vomiting, no weakness, no fever, no neck stiffness, no head injury. School performance is unchanged. The PIVOTAL clue, volunteered only when the candidate asks about medications: she was started on acne medication a few months ago - a 'tetracycline' tablet (doxycycline); if pressed you are unsure if it was that or 'the vitamin A one' (isotretinoin). She has acne and has been a bit down about teasing at school. Ideas: you are terrified she has a brain tumour. Concerns: her eyesight and her mood. Expectations: you want a scan and answers. Be anxious but cooperative.
candidate_instructions: You are the doctor in a rural clinic. A parent attends about their 15-year-old daughter, Samantha, who has had several weeks of worsening headache. In 8 minutes: take a focused history (from the parent), state your most likely diagnosis with reasoning, and outline your initial investigation and management plan including the medication issue. Address the parent's concerns.
examiner_instructions: Award marks for a complete SIQORAA headache history that screens paediatric red flags (early-morning vomiting, visual change, school decline, focal deficit) and, crucially, asks about VISION (blurring, diplopia, intracranial noises) and MEDICATIONS. The pass-defining step is eliciting the acne-medication link (tetracycline/isotretinoin) and connecting it to raised intracranial pressure. Expected diagnosis: idiopathic intracranial hypertension (avoid the outdated term 'benign'). Management: stop the triggering drug, urgent formal visual fields + fundoscopy/optic-disc assessment (ophthalmology - vision is the organ at risk), neuroimaging (MRI) with MR venography to exclude a mass and cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, then LP with opening-pressure measurement; acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) and weight loss; treat acne by another route. Mark communication for engaging the adolescent and reassuring the anxious parent.

criteria: Complete SIQORAA headache history from the parent with paediatric framing
Screens red flags: early-morning vomiting, focal deficit, school decline
Specifically asks about vision (blurring, diplopia) and intracranial noise
Asks about medications and elicits the acne-drug clue (tetracycline/isotretinoin)
Explores psychosocial impact of acne (mood, bullying, sleep)
States idiopathic intracranial hypertension using current terminology (not 'benign')
Justifies using the drug link, chronic headache, visual symptoms and mildly raised BP/BMI
Gives differentials (brain tumour, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, migraine, tension, refractive error)
Arranges urgent formal visual fields and fundoscopy/optic-disc assessment (ophthalmology)
Neuroimaging (MRI) plus MR venography and LP with opening-pressure measurement
Considers acetazolamide and weight loss; plans safe alternative acne therapy
Reassures the anxious parent and involves the adolescent with plain language
Provides safety-net advice to return/call 000 for worsening vision, focal deficit or reduced consciousness

red_flags: Progressive papilloedema / visual field loss or diplopia - threat of permanent vision loss requiring urgent ophthalmology and possible CSF diversion
Early-morning headache with vomiting, focal neurological deficit or school decline suggesting a space-occupying lesion (brain tumour)
Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis as an IIH mimic that must be excluded with MR venography
Reduced conscious level or new focal deficit - urgent neuroimaging and escalation
australian_guidelines: eTG / current neurology terminology: use idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) rather than 'benign' - untreated raised ICP can cause permanent visual loss; management centres on stopping causative drugs, weight loss and protecting vision

eTG isotretinoin safety: mandatory pregnancy prevention, teratogenicity counselling and mood monitoring when stopping/restarting acne therapy; tetracyclines are a recognised IIH trigger and should be ceased

RACGP acne management: first-line topical retinoids/topical antibiotics, oral tetracyclines short-course, combined oral contraceptive or spironolactone in women, oral isotretinoin under specialist supervision - choose a non-tetracycline route in IIH
Diagnostic pathway: neuroimaging (MRI) with MR venography to exclude a mass and venous sinus thrombosis, followed by LP with raised opening pressure and normal CSF constituents (confirmatory)
learning_objectives: Take a paediatric headache history that specifically screens vision and medication history
Link tetracyclines/isotretinoin and other drugs to idiopathic intracranial hypertension
Prioritise protection of vision with urgent ophthalmology assessment and appropriate imaging
Manage the causative acne medication safely while continuing acne care
key_points: Always ask a teenager with chronic headache about acne medication - tetracyclines and isotretinoin are classic IIH triggers
Vision is the organ at risk in IIH - urgent formal visual fields and optic-disc assessment are mandatory
MR venography is needed to exclude cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, an important IIH mimic
Acetazolamide is used for its CSF-lowering (carbonic-anhydrase-inhibiting) effect, not as a simple diuretic

citations.claim: Distinguishing raised-ICP causes (with red flags) from a normal-imaging pseudotumour picture requires the safe diagnostic strategy of excluding serious disorders.
A patient with red-flag headache features warrants neuroimaging (MRI) to exclude a brain tumour, which in IIH returns normal despite papilloedema.
Headache assessment in Australian primary care is grouped with attention to combined oral contraception and children as contributory factors, supporting the medication/OCP link to IIH.
